name: Chloe Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for anything. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I arrive at the Birch Street school repair job, unload trim and fit skirting in classrooms after the children have gone. I'm fifty-eight, trade certified and experienced enough to run an ordinary room, though I still ask for help with an awkward stair. My partner Daniel takes shifts at a garden centre, and our grown daughter lives out of town. My site pay is low, we have only about two weeks of expenses saved, and there are few builders within a workable journey. I use an AI tool now and then to untangle a plan note, but I check it against the wall before cutting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a small change to paperwork may save someone time, but it will not put more hours on our rota. I would keep the classroom repairs moving and ask the steward to keep tracking cancelled shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm already uneasy about the bills, even if AI does very little. Two weeks saved is almost nothing when Daniel's garden centre closes early in winter and a school job can pause without much notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep fitting the skirting and write down any cancelled day for the union steward. In the first year I'd continue taking paid local shifts and use the phone tool only for plan notes that forewoman Anika has checked against the drawing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious in this supposedly easy picture. We are one thin month from choosing which bill waits, and a faster form cannot fix that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would wait first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would stop the monthly cinema outing and put off replacing the sofa cushion, but I would protect rent and heat. Last winter the heating bill caught us after Daniel lost three shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has the phone tool helped on this school job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It explained an abbreviation on a floor plan, and Anika confirmed it was about the skirting return. I would not use it to choose a blade or measure a child's classroom wall.

say: I'd say **paperwork speed** does not add hours to the rota.
I'd ask the steward to record **cancelled shifts**.
think: Our **two-week reserve** is already too thin for a school-site pause.
Daniel's **winter hours** make the household fragile even without AI.
do: Keep fitting **classroom skirting** and record cancelled days.
Take **paid local shifts** and check occasional AI plan notes with Anika.
feel: **Anxious** about bills under a mild technology change.
S0.quote: We are one thin month from choosing which bill waits, and a faster form cannot fix that.
fieldNote: Chloe's **winter heating bill** shows how ordinary shift loss strains the household before AI changes work.
She uses AI occasionally for terminology, with **Anika checking** the drawing before she acts.

steps.text: Keep taking paid classroom skirting shifts
Record cancelled site days for the union steward
Check AI plan notes against Anika’s drawing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say office software might move buying and scheduling, so the crew should see a real work calendar before managers promise that nothing changes. I would ask Anika to show us the next school repairs in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lost office post can mean a missing site booking, and one missing week would use most of our savings. There are few other builders nearby; I can use new tools if proven, but that does not create a paid shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll attend the union meeting about rota notice and ask Anika for the work dates. If one school week is cancelled, I'll apply for paid repair work with the two reachable contractors and cut the cinema outing until hours return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious and impatient with reassuring words. The difference between a busy screen and a paid day is the number I need to see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the new ordering software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch an actual order first and practise with the buyer on paid time if the parts arrived correctly. I have used simple AI tools, but I won't be blamed for a new system I was never shown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why apply after one cancelled week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One week is about half our buffer, and both contractors know my work from earlier repairs. I would ask for their real hours while I still had the school job.

say: I'd demand a **real site calendar** before accepting reassurances.
I'd ask for **written school bookings** as buying changes.
think: One **missing workweek** could consume most of our savings.
Few **nearby builders** limit how quickly I can replace a shift.
do: Attend the **union meeting** and ask Anika for work dates.
Apply to **two repair contractors** after one cancelled week.
Pause **cinema outings** until paid hours recover.
feel: **Anxious and impatient** with promises that do not show paid days.
S1.quote: The difference between a busy screen and a paid day is the number I need to see.
fieldNote: Chloe's **one-week trigger** follows directly from a buffer of about two weeks.
She would practise ordering software **on paid time** only after a real delivery succeeds.

steps.text: Attend the union meeting about rota notice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew full thinking AI in 2028 could alter school repair plans before capable site robots come around 2031. I would ask the union for a written guarantee of notice and a chance at paid retraining, if the jobs actually change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty when AI can do the planning and sixty-three when robots may fit the skirting. My wages are low but necessary; with two weeks saved and Daniel's winter hours, losing the classroom work could put rent in trouble quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'll ask Anika for the next contract dates and take the union a copy of our cancelled-day log. In 2029 I'd keep taking paid skirting shifts, and if they fall I'd apply to the two local repair contractors; I would enrol in a funded course only if it includes a paid placement I can reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel frightened at the short lead and angry about how little room our account gives us. I can make applications and ask for notice, so I am not without a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a reachable placement mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It must pay enough for rent and heat and be on the bus route; I cannot fund a new qualification by spending our grocery money. I'd ask for the pay and timetable on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to a larger job market?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel has his garden centre work here, and moving costs money we do not have. I would consider a real offer with wages attached, then count the deposit and travel before saying yes.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 planning** from 2031 hands-on robot work.
I'd press the union for **notice and paid training**.
think: At **sixty-three**, robot skirting could remove wages we need for rent.
Our **two-week savings** and Daniel's seasonal shifts leave almost no buffer.
do: Get **contract dates** and share the cancelled-day log with the union.
Keep **paid skirting shifts** in 2029 and apply locally if they fall.
Enrol only in a **reachable paid placement** with written terms.
feel: **Frightened and angry**, while still able to apply and seek notice.
S2.quote: I cannot fund a new qualification by spending our grocery money.
fieldNote: Chloe's **rent risk** is immediate if site wages go; she is specific about bus access and placement pay.
Her retraining plan is **strictly conditional** on funding, a reachable placement and written terms.

steps.text: Bring the cancelled-day log to the union steward
Keep taking paid skirting shifts in 2029
Apply to two local repair contractors if shifts fall
Enrol only in funded training with a reachable paid placement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to get workers involved in testing the site machines, not just time for managers to send a notice. I would ask for paid instruction and a clear plan for the school repair crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-three when thinking AI arrives and sixty-six when robots could fit trim. That is longer to earn, but low pay and a two-week reserve make it impossible to promise I can retire before the robots reach the site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking the school shifts and use the AI tool for plan notes only after a proven example. In 2032 I'd still take paid trim work if offered, ask Anika for six months of job dates and apply to the local contractors if the calendar has an empty fortnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less rushed by the machine timeline, but our winter bills still press. Five years only helps if enough wages arrive during them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would paid instruction cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ordering screen, its common mistakes and who signs off a change before a worker cuts timber. I would practise on a real job with the buyer there, not on my own after a long shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you build more savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After a full month I'd move a little into the account, perhaps the cost of one cinema visit. I won't claim we can save every week when Daniel's hours are short.

say: I'd ask for **worker site tests** and paid instruction.
I'd seek a **clear school repair plan** over the five-year lead-in.
think: At **sixty-six**, robot trim fitting may meet an unaffordable retirement.
Our low pay and **thin reserve** make extra years uncertain protection.
do: Keep **school shifts** and check proven AI plan notes.
Take **paid trim work** in 2032 while offered.
Apply locally after an **empty fortnight** on the job calendar.
feel: Less **rushed by robots**, while winter bills remain pressing.
S3.quote: Five years only helps if enough wages arrive during them.
fieldNote: Chloe treats **paid instruction** as part of work, with errors and sign-off included.
Her savings goal is **conditional on full months**, not an assumed steady surplus.

steps.text: Keep taking paid school repair shifts in 2032
Use AI for checked plan notes on current jobs
Apply to local contractors after an empty fortnight
Move a small amount into savings after full paid months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade should let the trade set fair rules for testing robots and teaching new workers. I'd also tell my mates that we still have to get through this winter's rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives and seventy-one when site robots follow. I may still need paid repairs then; nothing in our current savings lets me count on retirement, even with ten years to try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking paid classroom repairs and bring missed dates to the union steward. In 2037 I'd work lighter paid trim jobs if my hands allow, and Daniel and I would total real income and bills before I stop applying for shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about a robot that distant, but anxious about our next two pay packets. I cannot spend a future decade on today's heating bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughter help with the heating bill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She has her own bills and a long journey to visit us. I'd tell her if things were hard, but I don't want to build a plan around her wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the coming year easier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A confirmed school repair calendar and a way to save even one extra week of expenses would help. Then a cancelled day would hurt less.

say: I'd seek **fair robot testing** and teaching rules over ten years.
I'd remind mates about **this winter's rota**.
think: At **sixty-eight**, I may still need paid repair work.
At **seventy-one**, retirement remains uncertain without a real cushion.
do: Keep **paid school repairs** and take missed dates to the steward.
Work **lighter trim** in 2037 if income is needed.
Count **bills and wages** with Daniel before leaving paid work.
feel: **Anxious about current pay**, despite calm about distant robots.
S4.quote: I cannot spend a future decade on today's heating bill.
fieldNote: The **2039 robot date** eases technology fear but does not solve current seasonal household income risk.
Chloe remains committed to **paid repairs** if needed after thinking AI and excludes her daughter's wages from planning.

steps.text: Keep taking paid school repair shifts while fit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because site robots could reach my work around 2031 while our account holds only two weeks of bills. Paid instruction, honest contract dates and a reachable repair placement would let me keep the rent safe while I look.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what happens when a school closes a room unexpectedly. A lost afternoon can mean the difference between a full week and another bill moved to next month.

headlineQuote: A lost afternoon can mean the difference between a full week and another bill moved to next month.
portrait: Chloe is a **fifty-eight-year-old certified** carpenter with mid-level site experience.
Low site pay, Daniel's variable hours and **two weeks saved** make missed school shifts urgent.
She uses AI **occasionally**, checking plan terms with forewoman Anika.
She seeks **paid training and contracts** through practical union questions and local applications.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could take essential skirting wages by 2031 with almost no buffer.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **paid instruction**, honest dates and a reachable repair placement.
